questions.title: Sodium Chloride
questions.stem: What is the typical adult bolus dose of sodium chloride for fluid resuscitation?
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride for fluid resuscitation is titrated to desired effect per patient presentation; the typical adult bolus falls in the 250 – 500 mL range, while 10 – 20 mL is the pediatric bolus range.

questions.title: Sodium Chloride
questions.stem: What is the typical pediatric bolus dose of sodium chloride for fluid resuscitation?
questions.explanation: The pediatric column lists a typical bolus range of 10 – 20 mL, titrated to desired effect; 250 – 500 mL is the adult range and giving it to a small child risks volume overload.

questions.title: Sodium Chloride
questions.stem: Sodium chloride solutions above which concentration should ideally be administered through a central line?
questions.explanation: Solutions greater than 2% should ideally go through a central line because of their osmolarity, though in an emergency a peripheral venous line may be used. Concentrated solutions above 1% are already considered irritants.

questions.title: Sodium Chloride
questions.stem: How much sodium does one liter of normal saline (0.9%) contain?
questions.explanation: Normal saline is the most commonly administered sodium chloride preparation, and each liter carries 9 grams (154 mEq) of sodium. A liter of 3% hypertonic saline carries 30 grams.

questions.title: Sodium Chloride
questions.stem: How many milliequivalents of sodium are in one liter of 3% hypertonic saline?
questions.explanation: A liter of 3% hypertonic saline contains 30 grams (513 mEq) of sodium, roughly three times the 154 mEq in a liter of normal saline — the reason it is hyperosmolar.

questions.title: Sodium Chloride
questions.stem: Which sodium chloride preparation is described as typically used to treat head injuries and cerebral edema?
questions.explanation: Hypertonic saline (3%) is hyperosmolar and draws water out of the injured brain, which is why it is the preparation named for head injury and cerebral edema; 0.9% normal saline is the routine resuscitation fluid.

questions.title: Sodium Chloride
questions.stem: What is the pharmacologic category of sodium chloride?
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride is classed as a parenteral electrolyte supplement; sodium is the principal extracellular cation and governs fluid balance, osmotic pressure and water distribution.

questions.title: Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate
questions.stem: What is the adult dose of sodium polystyrene sulfonate for hyperkalemia?
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia is the single listed indication, and the adult dose is 30 grams given orally or rectally; the weight-based 1 – 2 grams/kg is the pediatric dose.

questions.title: Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate
questions.stem: What is the pediatric dose of sodium polystyrene sulfonate for hyperkalemia?
questions.explanation: Children are dosed by weight at 1 – 2 grams/kg PO/PR for hyperkalemia; 30 grams is the fixed adult dose.

questions.title: Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate
questions.stem: How does sodium polystyrene sulfonate lower a patient's potassium?
options: It drives potassium into cells in exchange for hydrogen ions
It increases renal potassium excretion by blocking tubular reabsorption
It exchanges sodium ions for potassium ions in the intestine
It binds potassium in the bloodstream to form an inert complex
questions.explanation: The resin removes potassium by exchanging sodium ions for potassium ions in the intestine, so the potassium actually leaves the body in stool — which is also why it is slow and why it adds a sodium load.

questions.title: Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate
questions.stem: Which condition is a contraindication to sodium polystyrene sulfonate?
questions.explanation: Obstructive bowel disease is a listed contraindication because the resin must transit the gut to work and can cause fecal impaction. Severe heart failure and hypertension are cautions, not contraindications, because of the sodium load.

questions.title: Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate
questions.stem: Which electrolyte derangement is the warning for sodium polystyrene sulfonate specifically about?
questions.explanation: The warning states that severe hypokalemia may occur — the drug can overshoot and strip too much potassium. Hypernatremia, hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia are listed among its adverse reactions but are not the specific warning.

questions.title: Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate
questions.stem: What is the onset and duration of sodium polystyrene sulfonate?
questions.explanation: Onset is measured in hours with a 4 – 6 hour duration, so sodium polystyrene sulfonate does nothing for the unstable hyperkalemic patient in transport — calcium, insulin/dextrose and albuterol are the time-critical treatments.

questions.title: Succinylcholine
questions.stem: What is the adult dose of succinylcholine for paralysis for RSI?
questions.explanation: Adults are given 1 – 2 mg/kg IV for RSI paralysis, to a maximum of 200 mg. The flat 2 mg/kg figure is the pediatric dose and 3 – 4 mg IM is the combative-patient route.

questions.title: Succinylcholine
questions.stem: If succinylcholine is used for RSI in a patient under 10 years old, what is the dose?
questions.explanation: Children under 10 receive 2 mg/kg IV, max 200 mg — a higher per-kilogram dose than adults. The special considerations repeat this explicitly, since rocuronium is otherwise the agent of choice in that age group.

questions.title: Succinylcholine
questions.stem: What is the maximum dose of succinylcholine for RSI paralysis?
questions.explanation: Both the adult and pediatric RSI rows cap succinylcholine at 200 mg, so a large adult dosed at 2 mg/kg hits the ceiling at about 100 kg.

questions.title: Succinylcholine
questions.stem: What is the adult dose of succinylcholine for a combative patient without IV access when there are extreme safety-of-flight concerns?
questions.explanation: The combative-patient-without-IV-access row lists 3 – 4 mg IM, max 200 mg with no more than 5 mL per injection site. There is no LFN standing order for this indication in pediatric patients.

questions.title: Succinylcholine
questions.stem: What is the maximum volume of succinylcholine that may be given per injection site when dosing a combative patient intramuscularly?
questions.explanation: The IM route for a combative patient without IV access is capped at 200 mg total and 5 mL per injection site, so a larger volume must be split between sites.

questions.title: Succinylcholine
questions.stem: What is the pharmacologic category of succinylcholine?
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker: it mimics acetylcholine at the motor endplate, producing fasciculations and then sustained flaccid paralysis. Vecuronium and rocuronium are the non-depolarizing agents.

questions.title: Succinylcholine
questions.stem: Which history is a contraindication to succinylcholine?
questions.explanation: A history of malignant hyperthermia is a listed contraindication, alongside hyperkalemia, subacute burns, multiple sclerosis, ALS, crush injury, muscular dystrophy and spinal cord injury less than 6 months old — all conditions where succinylcholine risks lethal potassium release or triggering MH.

questions.title: Succinylcholine
questions.stem: Which paralytic is the agent of choice for RSI in pediatric patients under 10 years old?
questions.explanation: Rocuronium is preferred under 10 years old because of the rare risk of acute rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalemia with succinylcholine in undiagnosed myopathies; succinylcholine is still used for emergency intubation or when the airway must be secured immediately, such as laryngospasm.

questions.title: Succinylcholine
questions.stem: What is the antidote for malignant hyperthermia triggered by succinylcholine?
questions.explanation: Dantrolene is named as the antidote for malignant hyperthermia, which succinylcholine can trigger along with hyperkalemia.

questions.title: Succinylcholine
questions.stem: What are the onset and duration of succinylcholine?
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine takes effect in 30-60 seconds and wears off in about 8 minutes, which is the whole reason it is chosen for RSI; vecuronium's 2-3 minute onset and 30-45 minute duration is the slow, long alternative.

questions.title: Tenecteplase
questions.stem: What is the adult dose of tenecteplase for ischemic stroke?
questions.explanation: Ischemic stroke is dosed by weight at 0.25 mg/kg IV with a 25 mg ceiling, unlike STEMI which uses fixed milligram amounts by weight band.

questions.title: Tenecteplase
questions.stem: What is the maximum dose of tenecteplase for ischemic stroke?
questions.explanation: The ischemic stroke row caps tenecteplase at 25 mg, so a patient over 100 kg still receives only 25 mg. The 30 – 50 mg figures belong to the STEMI weight bands.

questions.title: Tenecteplase
questions.stem: How is tenecteplase administered for STEMI?
options: Infused over 10 minutes through a dedicated line
Given as a single bolus over 5 seconds through a dedicated line
Given as a bolus followed by an infusion over 8 hours
Infused over 60 minutes through a dedicated line
questions.explanation: Tenecteplase is a single bolus over 5 seconds via a dedicated line; it is not an infusion, which is one of the practical advantages over older thrombolytics.

questions.title: Tenecteplase
questions.stem: What is the final concentration of tenecteplase after it is reconstituted per the guideline?
questions.explanation: The full 10 mL of supplied sterile water is injected into the TNKase vial, giving a final concentration of 50 mg/10 mL — so the volume drawn in milliliters is one fifth of the milligram dose.

questions.title: Tenecteplase
questions.stem: Which diluent is used to reconstitute tenecteplase?
questions.explanation: The 10 mL of sterile water supplied with the kit is used; bacteriostatic water is explicitly prohibited, and the vial is swirled gently rather than shaken.

questions.title: Tenecteplase
questions.stem: Tenecteplase is incompatible with which solution, requiring the line to be flushed before and after administration?
questions.explanation: Tenecteplase is incompatible with dextrose, so dextrose-containing lines must be flushed with normal saline before and after the bolus.

questions.title: Tenecteplase
questions.stem: Which condition is a contraindication to tenecteplase?
questions.explanation: Active internal bleeding is listed, along with intracranial surgery or trauma within the last 2 months, intracranial aneurysm, coagulation disorder, severe uncontrolled hypertension and recent GI/GU bleeding — all settings where lysing clot risks catastrophic hemorrhage.

questions.title: Tenecteplase
questions.stem: What is the pharmacologic category of tenecteplase?
questions.explanation: Tenecteplase is a thrombolytic: it binds fibrin and converts tissue plasminogen to plasmin, promoting fibrinolysis. Ticagrelor is the antiplatelet and TXA is the antifibrinolytic — the opposite effect.

questions.title: Tenecteplase
questions.stem: Which adverse reaction to tenecteplase should the crew be watching for in flight after a STEMI bolus?
questions.explanation: Coronary thrombolysis may result in reperfusion arrhythmias; intracranial hemorrhage, bleeding and hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis are the other reactions to monitor for during and for several hours after administration.

questions.title: Terbutaline
questions.stem: What is the adult dose of terbutaline for preterm labor?
questions.explanation: Preterm labor is treated with 0.25 mg SQ, repeated every 30 minutes until tocolysis is achieved or a maximum of 3 doses. The 10 mcg/kg weight-based dosing belongs to the pediatric asthma row.

questions.title: Terbutaline
questions.stem: How often may terbutaline be repeated for preterm labor, and to what maximum?
options: Every 20 minutes to a maximum of 3 total doses
Every 30 minutes to a maximum of 3 doses
Every 30 minutes to a maximum of 2 doses
Every 10 minutes to a maximum of 3 doses
questions.explanation: Terbutaline for preterm labor is repeated every 30 minutes until tocolysis is achieved or a maximum of 3 doses is reached; the every-20-minute interval is the pediatric asthma schedule.

questions.title: Terbutaline
questions.stem: What is the pediatric dose of terbutaline for asthma in extremis?
questions.explanation: Asthma in extremis in a child is treated with 10 mcg/kg SQ/IM, or the same 10 mcg/kg IV given over 10 minutes. There is no LFN standing order for terbutaline in adult asthma.

questions.title: Terbutaline
questions.stem: What is the maximum single dose of terbutaline for a pediatric patient with asthma in extremis?
questions.explanation: The pediatric asthma row caps terbutaline at 400 mcg per dose by SC, IM or IV route, so a child over 40 kg receives the ceiling rather than the full 10 mcg/kg.

questions.title: Terbutaline
questions.stem: How often may terbutaline be repeated in a pediatric patient with asthma in extremis, and to what maximum?
options: Every 20 minutes PRN, maximum 3 total doses
Every 30 minutes PRN, maximum 3 total doses
Every 20 minutes PRN, maximum 2 total doses
Every 10 minutes PRN, maximum 3 total doses
questions.explanation: The pediatric asthma dose may be repeated every 20 minutes PRN for a maximum of 3 total doses; the 30-minute interval belongs to the adult preterm labor row.

questions.title: Terbutaline
questions.stem: What is the pharmacologic category of terbutaline?
questions.explanation: Terbutaline is a beta-2 agonist that raises intracellular cAMP, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle and inhibiting inflammatory mediator release — the same receptor action that relaxes the uterus in preterm labor.

questions.title: Terbutaline
questions.stem: What is the recommended mixture for terbutaline?
questions.explanation: Terbutaline is mixed 1 mg in 100 mL. Knowing the concentration matters because the pediatric IV dose is given over 10 minutes rather than pushed.

questions.title: Terbutaline
questions.stem: Which adverse reaction should be anticipated after giving terbutaline?
questions.explanation: As a sympathomimetic, terbutaline causes palpitations and tachyarrhythmias, along with hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, tremor and, paradoxically, bronchospasm and pulmonary edema.

questions.title: Ticagrelor
questions.stem: What is the adult dose of ticagrelor for STEMI?
questions.explanation: STEMI is the only listed indication and the adult loading dose is 180 mg PO. There is no LFN standing order for ticagrelor in pediatric patients.

questions.title: Ticagrelor
questions.stem: What is the pharmacologic category of ticagrelor?
questions.explanation: Ticagrelor is an antiplatelet agent, given alongside — not in place of — reperfusion therapy in STEMI. Tenecteplase is the thrombolytic on the adjacent page.

questions.title: Ticagrelor
questions.stem: By what mechanism does ticagrelor reduce platelet aggregation?
options: It reversibly binds the ADP P2Y12 receptor on the platelet surface
It irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase in the platelet
It directly blocks the GPIIb/IIIa receptor
It binds fibrin and converts plasminogen to plasmin
questions.explanation: Ticagrelor reversibly and noncompetitively binds the ADP P2Y12 receptor, preventing ADP-mediated activation of the GPIIb/IIIa complex downstream. Binding fibrin and converting plasminogen is tenecteplase's mechanism.

questions.title: Ticagrelor
questions.stem: Which history is a contraindication to ticagrelor?
questions.explanation: A history of intracranial hemorrhage is contraindicated, as are active bleeding, CABG surgery and severe hepatic impairment — all bleeding-risk considerations for an antiplatelet load.

questions.title: Ticagrelor
questions.stem: Which adverse reaction is listed for ticagrelor that may be mistaken for a worsening cardiac presentation?
questions.explanation: Dyspnea is a recognised ticagrelor effect and can be misread as heart failure or a worsening infarct; nausea, hemorrhage and dizziness are the other listed reactions.

questions.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
questions.stem: What is the adult dose of TXA for severe trauma likely to require massive transfusion?
questions.explanation: The adult dose is 2 grams, mixed with 100 mL of normal saline and infused over 10 minutes, with a maximum of 2 grams. Some hospitals use a 1-gram bolus plus an 8-hour infusion instead — if that was started before arrival, continue it.

questions.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
questions.stem: How is the adult TXA dose prepared and delivered for severe trauma?
options: Mixed with 100 mL of NS and infused over 10 minutes
Given as a single bolus over 5 seconds
Mixed with 100 mL of NS and infused over 8 hours
Given undiluted as a slow IV push over 2 minutes
questions.explanation: TXA is mixed with 100 mL of normal saline and infused over 10 minutes; rapid infusion may cause hypotension, which is why it is not pushed.

questions.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
questions.stem: What is the pediatric dose of TXA for severe trauma likely to require massive transfusion?
questions.explanation: Children receive 15 mg/kg mixed in 100 mL NS over 10 minutes, capped at 1 gram — half the adult 2-gram ceiling.

questions.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
questions.stem: Within what time from injury must TXA be given under LFN guidelines without additional orders?
questions.explanation: LFN guidelines require the injury to have occurred 2 hours or less prior; giving TXA outside that window requires medical consult or orders from the sending provider.

questions.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
questions.stem: What takes priority over TXA administration in the severely injured trauma patient?
options: Obtaining a second IV access site
Blood administration and other life threats
Documenting the exact time of injury
questions.explanation: Blood administration and the treatment of other life threats must take priority over TXA — TXA supports clot stability but does not replace resuscitation.

questions.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
questions.stem: What line precaution applies when giving TXA to a patient receiving a transfusion?
options: It must be given through a central line only
It should not be administered in the same line as blood products
The line must be flushed with dextrose before and after
It must be given through a filtered line
questions.explanation: TXA should not be administered in the same line as blood products, so a second access point or a dedicated lumen is needed when both are running.

questions.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
questions.stem: Which condition is a contraindication to TXA?
questions.explanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage and thromboembolic disease are the listed contraindications — in both, stabilising clot carries its own harm.

questions.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
questions.stem: What is the pharmacologic category of TXA?
questions.explanation: TXA is an antifibrinolytic and hemostatic agent: it competitively inhibits plasminogen activation, preventing the breakdown of clot that has already formed — the exact opposite of tenecteplase.

questions.title: Vasopressin
questions.stem: What is the adult dose of vasopressin for shock or hypotension refractory to norepinephrine?
questions.explanation: Vasopressin runs at a fixed 0.03 units/min rather than being titrated, and it is added only once norepinephrine has failed to correct the shock state. There is no LFN standing order for pediatric patients.

questions.title: Vasopressin
questions.stem: Under what circumstance does the formulary call for vasopressin?
options: Hypotension in the setting of head injury
Shock or hypotension refractory to norepinephrine
Shock or hypotension refractory to fluid bolus alone
questions.explanation: Vasopressin's single listed indication is shock or hypotension that is refractory to norepinephrine, so it is a second-line vasopressor added on top of a running norepinephrine infusion.

questions.title: Vasopressin
questions.stem: What is the recommended mixture for a vasopressin infusion?
questions.explanation: Vasopressin is mixed 20 units in 100 mL, which at the standing 0.03 units/min rate works out to a very low infusion rate — worth double-checking on the pump.

questions.title: Vasopressin
questions.stem: What is the pharmacologic category of vasopressin?
questions.explanation: Vasopressin is an antidiuretic hormone analog that also acts as an inotrope/vasopressor, which is why it raises pressure through a different receptor pathway than the catecholamine norepinephrine it is added to.

questions.title: Vasopressin
questions.stem: Which adverse reaction is listed for vasopressin?
questions.explanation: Angina and hypertension are the listed adverse reactions — vasopressin's intense vasoconstriction can compromise coronary perfusion, so watch the monitor and the 12-lead in a patient with coronary disease.

questions.title: Vecuronium
questions.stem: What is the adult dose of vecuronium for paralysis of the intubated patient?
questions.explanation: Vecuronium is dosed at 0.1 mg/kg and may be repeated PRN to maintain paralysis of an already intubated patient; the 1 – 2 mg/kg figure belongs to succinylcholine for RSI.

questions.title: Vecuronium
questions.stem: What is the pediatric dose of vecuronium for paralysis of the intubated patient?
questions.explanation: The pediatric column reads "same as adults," so children also receive 0.1 mg/kg and may be redosed PRN — unlike succinylcholine, which has a separate pediatric figure and an age restriction.

questions.title: Vecuronium
questions.stem: What is the pharmacologic category of vecuronium?
questions.explanation: Vecuronium is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker: it blocks acetylcholine from binding at the motor endplate, so there are no fasciculations and none of succinylcholine's hyperkalemia or malignant hyperthermia risk.

questions.title: Vecuronium
questions.stem: What are the onset and duration of vecuronium?
questions.explanation: Vecuronium takes 2-3 minutes to work and lasts 30-45 minutes, so it is a maintenance paralytic for an already secured airway rather than an induction agent, and sedation must be running well before it is given.

questions.title: Vecuronium
questions.stem: Which adverse reaction is listed for vecuronium?
questions.explanation: Apnea, dysrhythmias, transient hypotension and tachycardia are the listed reactions. Fasciculations and hyperkalemia belong to succinylcholine, the depolarizing agent.
